source.title: Dissecting U-net for Seismic Application: An In-Depth Study on Deep Learning Multiple Removal
source.authors: Ricard Durall; A. Ghanim; N. Ettrich; Janis Keuper

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper compares training choices and network depth, then evaluates outcomes on synthetic validation data and real seismic data. This is a conceptual test of optimizer and model-size effects on generalization, using seismic demultiple quality rather than a train/test error gap.
record.gate_note: Rows cover the paper's own optimizer and depth results. Other hyperparameter comparisons (sampling, kernel size, and loss objective) are also included where the paper reports an outcome; cited optimizer findings are not treated as this study's results.
record.test_reason: The study compares Adam with momentum SGD on synthetic validation and unseen real seismic data, extending V4's optimizer comparison to seismic image restoration. Held-out performance can bear on V4 without a numerical training–test gap, although the optimizer tuning protocol is unspecified.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's optimizer and depth paraphrase is accurate: Adam improves synthetic validation metrics but produces less reliable real-data outcomes, motivating momentum SGD; the standard U-net provides the preferred quality–size trade-off. More broadly, the authors conclude that their synthetic-trained model removes multiples while preserving seismic characteristics on field data, while acknowledging that their hyperparameter analysis covers only a subset of configurations.
record.recipe_differences: The paper trains a seismic U-net on synthetic multiple-infested and multiple-free gather pairs and evaluates demultiple outcomes on synthetic validation and real seismic data. It does not use random labels, natural-image classification, or train/test error gaps.
record.method_sensitivity: Optimizer choice changes synthetic-validation versus real-data outcomes; kernel size affects over-smoothing and sensitivity to initialization; depth changes demultiple capacity and quality–size trade-off. Sampling technique and direct versus inverse objective show similar outcomes.

fits_no_version.finding: Sampling combinations perform similarly, with max-pooling and bilinear interpolation producing the most stable runs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sampling operations can affect run stability without materially changing seismic demultiple performance.

fits_no_version.finding: The smallest kernel sequence improves qualitative results; larger pooling kernels can over-smooth and increase initialization sensitivity.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: More aggressive pooling can impair seismic-event preservation despite similar validation metrics.

fits_no_version.finding: Direct and inverse prediction objectives yield similar validation results.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Predicting clean gathers or predicting multiples for subtraction can produce comparable demultiple outcomes.

fits_no_version.finding: The small U-net underperforms, while the big U-net offers no further improvement over the standard model.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Increasing U-net depth helps up to the standard topology in this task, with further depth adding computational cost without reported quality gains.

record.problems: The optimizer results are largely qualitative, with exact metric values shown only in figures. The study evaluates seismic demultiple quality rather than classification train/test error. It averages validation results over five runs but reports no explicit uncertainty values for the metrics. The kernel result text appears inconsistent with Table 1's case D configuration.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows for individual validation metric values because the plots are not numerically transcribed in the supplied text. No rows for field-example comparisons in Figures 9–10, which compare demultiple methods rather than the claim versions' training/generalization gap.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and natural-label versus random-label held-out accuracy.
Width increases beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected architectures and the contribution of local connectivity.
Image-classification and language benchmarks; a documented limited-versus-broader tuning comparison; comparative training performance; decoupled weight decay; switching optimizers.
Batch-size comparisons under fixed epoch budgets and adapted training recipes.
Dropout effects and interactions with dataset size, augmentation, and weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness, generalization gaps, and ranking against alternative measures.
Removing memorized examples versus removing random examples and retraining.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source for V4. Real-data evaluation lacks ground truth and uses qualitative inspection. The discussion also reports iterative synthetic-data development informed by real-data outcomes, so these results do not establish an untouched real-data test evaluation.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label test accuracy.
Width sweep past the interpolation threshold.
Comparison of convolutional and fully connected networks.
Limited-tuning comparison on image-classification or language benchmarks; equal training performance and explicit weight-decay or optimizer-switch interventions.
Large versus small batch sizes under fixed epoch budgets.
Dropout and its interaction with training set size, augmentation, and weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and comparisons with norm- and margin-based measures.
Removal of memorized training examples and resulting test accuracy.

rows.subject: model trained with Adam optimizer
rows.stage_stated: trained on synthetic pairs; five independent runs
rows.operation_detail: Train with Adam optimizer and assess demultiple results on synthetic validation data and real data.
rows.measure: MSE, SNR, SSIM and PCORR validation metrics; paper says Adam reaches better values than SGD in synthetic validation plots.
rows.baseline: SGD with momentum; numerical values not stated in text.
rows.value: Adam converges faster and the metrics reach better values; exact values are figure-only.
rows.uncertainty: Validation results averaged over five independent runs; error bars not stated.
rows.note: The text states a metric advantage but gives no numerical train/test generalization gap; Figure 3a is not transcribed.
rows.check: Adam achieves better synthetic validation metrics, opposite to the adaptive-optimizer disadvantage. The explicit textual comparison establishes direction despite unavailable figure values. Validation metrics do not establish better training loss or a lower training-loss minimum.

source_check.locator_found: Section 3, validation protocol; Section 3.1, synthetic validation comparison; Figure 3a.

rows.subject: model trained with Adam optimizer
rows.stage_stated: trained on synthetic pairs; varying among different runs
rows.operation_detail: Train with Adam and infer on real seismic data.
rows.measure: Real-data demultiple quality: primary-energy preservation and residual-multiple suppression.
rows.baseline: SGD optimizer; exact numeric baseline not stated.
rows.value: Adam tends to fail to generalize more often; results are inconsistent across runs, with occasional primary suppression and residual multiples.
rows.note: This is a stated real-data generalization comparison, but it does not report train/test error or a quantitative held-out performance gap.
rows.check: The authors explicitly report more frequent real-data generalization failures with Adam than SGD. Occasional failures and qualitative evidence do not themselves make this comparative effect partial; its magnitude and frequency remain unquantified.

rows.subject: model trained with SGD optimizer
rows.stage_stated: trained on synthetic pairs; five independent runs
rows.operation_detail: Train with SGD and compare its validation and real-data results with Adam.
rows.measure: MSE, SNR, SSIM and PCORR validation metrics; synthetic inference comparison.
rows.baseline: Adam; synthetic inference differences described as negligible.
rows.value: Synthetic results are similar to Adam; differences in the two displayed validation gathers are negligible.
rows.uncertainty: Validation results averaged over five independent runs; error bars not stated.
rows.note: The paper gives a qualitative comparison, not train/test error values.
rows.check: Restrict this row to the two displayed synthetic gathers in Figure 3b, whose output differences are described as negligible. Figure 3a instead reports better aggregate validation metrics for Adam and is already covered by R1.

source_check.correct: Restrict the negligible-difference result to visual inference on the two synthetic validation gathers in Figure 3b; measure: qualitative demultiple output; state: absent. Five-run averaged MSE, SNR, SSIM and PCORR instead favor Adam in Figure 3a; state: reversed. The five-run averaging protocol is not stated for the displayed inference examples.
source_check.locator_found: Section 3, five-run validation protocol; Section 3.1, comparison of aggregate metrics and inspected synthetic results; Figure 3b caption.
source_check.problem: The row combines aggregate validation metrics favoring Adam with negligible visual differences on two displayed gathers, assigning one condition and state to different assessments.

rows.subject: model trained with SGD optimizer
rows.operation_detail: Train with SGD and infer on real seismic data.
rows.measure: Real-data demultiple quality: primary-energy preservation and residual-multiple suppression.
rows.baseline: Adam optimizer; exact numeric baseline not stated.
rows.value: Authors favour SGD because Adam can suppress primary energy and leave residual multiples on real data; SGD is shown as the preferred approach.
rows.note: Qualitative real-data result; no numeric gap or uncertainty is given.
rows.check: The qualitative real-data comparison supports an SGD advantage. This overlaps R2 and should not count as independent evidence; the authors' optimizer preference is a conclusion rather than an additional measurement.

rows.subject: U-net with max-pooling and bilinear sampling
rows.operation_detail: Compare down- and up-sampling combinations, including transposed convolutions, pooling, and interpolation.

conditions.value: max-pooling and bilinear are non-learnable methods

rows.measure: Validation metrics and stability of runs; synthetic and real-data inference.
rows.baseline: Other tested sampling configurations; exact values not stated.
rows.value: All sampling techniques reach similar performance; max-pooling plus bilinear gives the most stable results, and synthetic and real data show no difference among configurations.
rows.uncertainty: Five independent runs; uncertainty values not stated.
rows.note: Sampling-method effects do not fit a claim version.
rows.check: Sampling-method performance and run stability do not measure any listed version.

rows.subject: U-net with kernel sequence 11 22 22 22 (case A)
rows.stage_stated: trained; sensitivity to initial weights noted
rows.operation_detail: Train with the smaller max-pooling kernel sequence and compare kernel configurations.
rows.baseline: Larger-kernel configurations; exact numeric baseline not stated.
rows.value: Smaller-kernel configuration is among the configurations compared; the paper reports consistent improvement after quality control for case A and D using 11 22 22 22 sequence.
rows.note: The text gives a qualitative quality-control result without assigning a numeric magnitude to this case separately.
rows.check: No listed version concerns pooling kernels. The text attributes improvement to the 11 22 22 22 sequence, case A; Figure 5b compares A with D rather than reporting improvement for both.

rows.subject: U-net with kernel sequence 12 24 24 24 (case B)
rows.stage_stated: trained; sensitivity to initial weights noted
rows.operation_detail: Train with a more aggressive non-square kernel sequence.
rows.baseline: Smaller-kernel configurations; exact numeric baseline not stated.
rows.value: Larger max-pooling kernels remove multiples more aggressively and over-smooth results; larger-kernel models appear more sensitive to initial weights.
rows.note: The paper does not state a numerical measure for this configuration.
rows.check: Kernel effects fit no version. Over-smoothing and initialization sensitivity are reported for larger kernels collectively, without a separately stated case-B effect.

rows.subject: U-net with kernel sequence 22 22 22 22 (case C)
rows.stage_stated: trained; sensitivity to initial weights noted
rows.operation_detail: Train with a square kernel sequence and compare kernel configurations.
rows.baseline: Smaller-kernel configurations; exact numeric baseline not stated.
rows.value: Larger max-pooling kernels remove multiples more aggressively and over-smooth results; larger-kernel models appear more sensitive to initial weights.
rows.note: The paper does not state a numerical measure for this configuration.
rows.check: Kernel effects fit no version. The text does not separately establish the reported larger-kernel effects for case C, which Table 1 labels low aggressiveness.

rows.subject: U-net with kernel sequence 24 24 24 24 (case D)
rows.stage_stated: trained; sensitivity to initial weights noted
rows.operation_detail: Train with the more aggressive square kernel sequence.
rows.baseline: Smaller-kernel configurations; exact numeric baseline not stated.
rows.value: Case D, using the 11 22 22 22 sequence as printed in the result description, is reported as consistently improved after quality control; larger kernels generally remove multiples more aggressively and over-smooth.
rows.note: The result text's case/sequence wording is internally inconsistent with Table 1, so this result cannot be assigned confidently to the listed case D sequence.
rows.check: The claimed case-D improvement is incorrect. Table 1 assigns D the sequence 24 24 24 24; the prose attributes improvement only to 11 22 22 22, case A. Figure 5b displays A and D as comparators, creating no case-to-sequence contradiction.

rows.subject: small U-net
rows.operation_detail: Reduce depth by removing two down-sampling and two up-sampling layers from the standard topology.
rows.measure: Demultiple quality; ability to suppress multiples without over-smoothing.
rows.baseline: standard U-net; exact metric values not stated.
rows.value: Too shallow and lacks capacity to suppress multiples without over-smoothing; metrics and real-data results underperform the standard model.
rows.note: The study reports qualitative underperformance; this is model depth, not width beyond an interpolation threshold.
rows.check: Depth and parameter-count comparisons do not test V2's width sweep beyond zero training error. The reported small-model underperformance is otherwise accurately paraphrased.

rows.subject: standard U-net
rows.operation_detail: Use as the baseline topology in the depth comparison.
rows.baseline: small and big U-net; exact quality values not stated.
rows.value: Authors describe the standard model as the optimal trade-off between quality and size; inference time 22.91 ± 0.02 s on 6000 images 64 × 256 pixels.
rows.note: The qualitative optimal-trade-off statement is reported, but it is not a width sweep or a train/test error measure.
rows.check: The preferred quality–size trade-off and inference time do not measure a listed version. The preference is an author conclusion rather than a separate performance measurement.

rows.subject: big U-net
rows.operation_detail: Increase depth by adding two down-sampling and two up-sampling layers to the standard topology.
rows.baseline: standard U-net; exact quality values not stated.
rows.value: Over-parameterized; extra layers offer no further improvement. Inference time 42.70 ± 0.01 s on 6000 images 64 × 256 pixels.
rows.note: Depth adds parameters but does not improve reported demultiple quality.
rows.check: No improvement from added depth does not establish absence of V2's width effect. Training interpolation is not measured.
